{{< include _copilot-disclaimer.qmd >}}

A mathematical paper is made of sentences, and the formulas are part of the sentences.
This chapter collects rules for fitting formulas into prose.
It draws on the lecture notes of a Stanford course on mathematical writing
[@knuth1987mathematical].
This chapter selects the rules that bear most on formulas.
Several of the course's other rules appear in other chapters,
and @tbl-knuth-elsewhere points to them.
The notes also cover spelling, punctuation and refereeing, which this book does not.

# Keep formulas inside sentences

Readers encounter a formula as part of a sentence,
so the words around it decide whether the formula can be read.

## Separate formulas with words

Put words between two formulas.
Without them, the reader cannot tell where one formula ends and the next begins.

::: {#exm-separate-formulas}

# Separating two formulas

> ❌ Define $f_k$, $k \ge 2$.
>
> ✅ Define $f_k$, where $k \ge 2$.

In the ❌ version the comma between the two formulas seems to belong to the first one.
The ✅ version names the relation between them.

:::

## Do not start a sentence with a symbol

A sentence that starts with a symbol is hard to see as a new sentence,
because the formula runs on from the period before it.
Start with a word, such as the name of the object.

::: {#exm-symbol-first}

# Starting a sentence with a word

> ❌ $t^2 - 5$ has two real roots.
>
> ✅ The polynomial $t^2 - 5$ has two real roots.

:::

## Write logical symbols as words

In prose, write "implies", "for every" and "there exists",
not $\Rightarrow$, $\forall$ and $\exists$.
The same goes for the symbols for "therefore" and "such that".
Keep the symbols in a work on logic.

## Test the sentence with the formulas removed

Many readers skim past the formulas on a first reading.
Replace each formula by a placeholder such as "blah".
If the sentence no longer reads smoothly,
rewrite it.

## Tie formulas together with commentary

A list of formulas with no words between them is the style of a homework paper.
Say what each step does and why the next one follows.
A sentence such as "Because the set $S$ has an element, we can pick one and call it $s$" tells the reader
where the argument is going, and the bare formula does not.

## Make the prose say what the formula says

The sentence that introduces or interprets a formula must describe that formula.
Check every [term](defining-terms.qmd#def-term) in the sentence against the formula, symbol by symbol.
The words and the symbols must name the same quantity, the same data, and the same kind of average.
When you change one, change the other in the same edit.

::: {#exm-prose-matches-math}

# A sentence that names the wrong average

Suppose the formula is $\E{\paren{\newoutvar - \predvalf{\predvar}}^2}$, a [population](defining-terms.qmd#def-population) mean at one covariate value $\predvar$.
The sentence "the average squared error over the training set" does not describe it.
It names a sample average over many observations.
Write "the expected squared prediction error at $\predvar$" instead.

:::

Before you submit, reread each formula next to the sentence that describes it.
Do the same after every edit to either one.
Related rules cover [using one notation for one thing](notation.qmd#matching-names-and-notation)
and [defining every variable when you introduce it](defining-terms.qmd#guidelines-for-defining-terms).

## Write each sentence in words or in math, not both

A sentence is either entirely in words or entirely in math.
A single inline expression inside a word sentence is fine,
as in "the prediction function $\predfn$ equals the conditional mean". <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
A sentence that states one condition in words and a second condition as a relation between expressions is a hybrid.
Split it into two complete sentences:
the first states the result in words, and the second states it as a displayed formula.

::: {#exm-no-hybrid-sentences}

# Splitting a hybrid sentence

> ❌ The reducible risk is zero if and only if $\P(\predfnf{\Predvar} \ne \E{\Outvar \mid \Predvar}) = 0$.
>
> ✅ The reducible risk is zero if and only if the prediction function differs from the conditional mean with probability 0. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
>
> $$
> \ba
> \E{\sqf{\condE{\Outvar}{\Predvar} - \predfnf{\Predvar}}} &= 0
> \\
> \iff \Pf{\predfnf{\Predvar} \ne \condE{\Outvar}{\Predvar}} &= 0
> \ea
> $$

The ❌ version puts the first condition in words and the second in math.
The ✅ version says the result once in words and once in math.

:::

## Give every relationship stated in words a formal expression

When a sentence states a mathematical relationship, also write that relationship as a formal expression.
A relationship is any claim that links quantities, such as:

- an equality or an inequality;
- a limit;
- a proportionality;
- a bound or an ordering;
- a "depends on".

Keep the sentence, because it tells the reader what the relationship means,
and add the displayed formula, because it tells the reader exactly what the relationship is.
Prose alone leaves the reader to guess the quantities, the direction, and the conditions.
Put every condition of the prose in the formula too, and introduce its symbols in the sentence.
Keep the sentence and the formula separate, as the rule to
[write each sentence in words or in math](#write-each-sentence-in-words-or-in-math-not-both) requires:
the display may follow a lead-in such as "In symbols:", and the formula is not part of the sentence in words.

::: {#exm-prose-relationship-formal}

# Adding the formula to a prose relationship

> ❌ If random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent, the [variance](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#def-variance) of their sum is the sum of their variances.
>
> ✅ If random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent, the variance of their sum is the sum of their variances.
> In symbols:
>
> $$X \ind Y \implies \Var{X + Y} = \Var{X} + \Var{Y}.$$

The ❌ version leaves the reader to reconstruct the formula and its condition.
The ✅ version keeps the sentence and adds the relationship in math,
with the independence condition inside the formula.

:::

# Introduce a theorem with a sentence

The line before a theorem, lemma or algorithm should be a complete sentence,
or end with a colon.
Do not let a heading such as "Theorem" finish a sentence that began above it.

::: {#exm-introduce-theorem}

# Introducing a theorem

> ❌ This gives the following
> **Theorem.** $G(x)$ is increasing.
>
> ✅ Next we prove a result about monotonicity.
> **Theorem.**
> The function $G(x)$ defined in equation (3) is increasing. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->

The ❌ version breaks a sentence across the theorem and starts the theorem with a symbol.
The ✅ version uses a complete sentence, and the theorem names its object.

:::

Write the statement of a theorem so that it stands alone.
A reader who jumps to the theorem should not need the assumptions in the paragraph before it,
so repeat them in the statement.

# Display and number the formulas that matter

Put each important formula on a line by itself.
Number the important ones, even if you do not refer to them,
because a reader may want to refer to them later.
Quarto's [equation cross-references](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html#equations)
number a display and let you link to it.

A key equation always goes in a display, never inline.
A key equation is any of these:

- the conclusion of a theorem, lemma, or proposition;
- an equation that a proof builds toward;
- an equation that a later step refers to.

In a proof, a sentence such as "so $A = B$" or "this gives $A = B$"
hides the result in the middle of a line.
Put the equation in a display and let the sentence introduce it.
Use inline math for symbols and short expressions inside a sentence,
not for the equation the reader is meant to remember.

::: {#exm-key-equation-displayed}

# Displaying the normal equations

> ❌ Setting the gradient to zero yields $\stprod{\design} \vcoef = \tp{\design} \vy$.
>
> ✅ Setting the gradient to zero yields the normal equations:
>
> $$\stprod{\design} \vcoef = \tp{\design} \vy$$

In the ❌ version the result sits in the middle of a line, where the reader can miss it.
The ✅ version gives it a line of its own.

:::

# Write numbers according to how they are used

Spell out a small number when it is an adjective:
"the proof uses three lemmas".
Write the numeral when the number is a name or a value:
"Lemma 3 is used 12 times", "the total rose by 4".
Capitalize the name of a numbered result, as in "Theorem 1" and "Lemma 2".

# Keep subscripts under control

Do not name the elements of a set unless you need to.
If you write "Let $X = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$",
you will need $x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_m}$ as soon as you take a subset of $X$.
A subscript on a subscript is hard to read.
Write "an element $x$ of $X$" instead,
and refer to $x$ and $y$ for two elements.
Use $x_1$ and $x_2$ only when you need two specified elements.

# Choose the voice and the person

Use "we" to mean the author and the reader together,
as in "we can now prove".
Write "we prove", not the passive "it can be proved".
Avoid "I" unless the author's persona is relevant.

Write "assume that $G$ is finite", not "assume $G$ is finite".
The word "that" helps the reader parse the sentence.
Do not write "we have that $y = z$"; write "we have $y = z$".

# Choose the proof that fits the claim

Do not use proof by contradiction where a direct proof will do.
The course's worked example proves a lemma both ways.
The direct proof is shorter,
and it does not assume that the entries are integers or restate their ordering.

# Cite results, not solutions

A proof, or any derivation that supports a result, never cites a solution to an exercise.
A solution answers an exercise for the reader who attempted the exercise,
so the solution is not a result that other arguments can build on.
Follow each solution that contains a reusable result with a result div (a theorem, lemma, corollary or proposition) that states the claim.
The test is whether the solution contains a result that other arguments could use,
not whether any later argument currently relies on it.
Cite that result div in every argument that uses the claim.

::: {#exm-cite-results}

# Citing a result div

> ❌ **Proof.**
> By Solution 9 and Solution 10, the claim holds.
>
> ✅ **Proof.**
> By Lemma 4 and Lemma 5, the claim holds.

The ❌ version sends the reader to answers that the notes may reorder, hide or drop.
The ✅ version cites claims that the notes state, number and keep.

:::

Add an exercise and its solution just before every result div that you add or edit.
The exercise does not state the result.
It asks the student to find the result, such as "find an expression for the spread of a random variable using its first two moments",
so that the reader discovers the result,
and the result div then states what the solution showed.
Every later argument cites the result div.

The one exception to the citation rule follows from that pairing:
the proof of the result itself may cite the solution of the exercise that asks for that same result.
Such a proof does no derivation of its own: it is the one line `By @sol-x.`, with one citation.
This is the one place where a proof cites a solution.
[Derivation format](defining-terms/derivation-format.qmd) describes the exercise, solution, theorem and proof pattern.
When the exercise has several parts, the line may cite each part, as in the line `By @sol-x and @sol-x-part2.`, which ends in a period.
A proof with its own steps or display math cites result divs instead.

The `check-solution-citations` workflow in [`Morrison-Lab/gha`](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/gha) flags a `@sol-` cross-reference inside a proof or result div.
It lets a one-line proof with one citation pass.
For a one-line proof that cites several parts of the paired solution, the HTML comment `<!-- check-solution-citations: allow -->` on that line tells the workflow to skip that line.
Quarto removes the comment from the rendered page.
The workflow does not check prose outside proof and result divs, but the rule still applies there.

# Keep each div minimal: cite, never inline

Every result div states one result and every solution div answers one exercise, and each does no more.
When a proof or a solution needs a step that a reader could use elsewhere, state that step as its own result div, preceded by its exercise and solution, and cite that result div.
Never derive the step inline.
A solution decomposes the same way: each solution is the smallest argument that answers its exercise, and it cites result divs for the steps that other arguments also use.

::: {#exm-never-inline}

# Citing a step instead of deriving it

> ❌ **Proof.**
> By the chain rule, $\gradwrt{\vcoef}{\resid_i^2} = 2 \resid_i \vfeatmap(\vx_i)$, where $\resid_i$ is the residual and $\vfeatmap(\vx_i)$ the design vector, and summing over $i$ gives the claim.
>
> ✅ **Proof.**
> Lemma 4 gives the gradient of each summand,
> and Lemma 5 says that the gradient of a sum is the sum of the gradients,
> so the gradient of the total is the sum of $2 \resid_i \vfeatmap(\vx_i)$ over $i$.

The ❌ proof derives inline the result that Lemma 4 states, so a reader who needs that step elsewhere has nowhere to cite.

:::

No div repeats reasoning that it could cite instead.
Two arguments that share a step cite one result div, so a correction to the step is made once.

No check can decide whether a step is reusable, so this rule stays a writing rule that review enforces.
The `check-solution-citations` workflow covers only the citation of solutions.

# Use no symbol that the statement does not need

Halmos advises "avoid the use of irrelevant symbols"
and states the rule in its showy form as "use no letter only once"
[@halmos1970write, section 15].
A symbol that appears once, in the sentence that introduces it,
adds a name for the reader to hold and nothing to use it for.
Delete the symbol, or use it in the statement that needs it.

:::{#exm-superfluous-symbol}

# Deleting a symbol that is named and never used

> ❌ Every continuous real-valued [function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/functions.html#def-function) $f$ on a compact space is bounded.
>
> ✅ Every continuous real-valued function on a compact space is bounded.

Nothing in the sentence refers to $f$ again,
so the symbol contributes nothing to the statement.
Halmos gives this sentence as his example
[@halmos1970write, section 15].

:::

When you apply a displayed relation to a second object, name the relation or restate it, rather than citing its tag.
Halmos calls "$g$ also satisfies (*)" "logical and alphabetical nonsense"
and advises "(*) remains satisfied if $f$ is replaced by $g$",
or, better, giving the relation a name
[@halmos1970write, section 15].
A named relation also lets the reader find it without hunting for a tag.

:::{#exm-name-the-relation}

# Naming the relation instead of tagging it

> ❌ The [sample mean](defining-terms.qmd#def-sample-mean) satisfies Equation 3, which says that the estimator's expected value equals the parameter.
> The sample [variance](defining-terms.qmd#def-variance-expression-and-prose) also satisfies Equation 3.
>
> ✅ The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the [population](defining-terms.qmd#def-population) mean.
> The sample variance is an unbiased estimator of the population variance.

In the ❌ version, "also satisfies Equation 3" is a statement about a different parameter,
and the equation says nothing about which parameter.
The ✅ version names the property, "unbiased",
and states each parameter.

:::

Halmos also says this rule "is sometimes better to break than to obey":
a symbol that you introduce so that a later sentence in the same paragraph can use it is not superfluous.
No check can tell a symbol that a later sentence uses from one that it never uses,
because "later" can span pages, so this stays a writing rule that review enforces.

# Repeat the wording of parallel results, then point out the difference

When a later result treats a parallel or more general case,
Halmos advises that "it is a big help to the reader
if you use the same words in the same order for as long as possible,
and then, with a proper roll of drums, emphasize the difference"
[@halmos1970write, section 11].
He adds that listing the shared conditions and dropping one is not enough;
say which condition changed
[@halmos1970write, section 11].

:::{#exm-parallel-wording}

# Defining the lasso in the words of the ridge definition

> ❌ The ridge estimate minimizes the [residual sum of squares](defining-terms.qmd#def-rss) plus a penalty on the size of the coefficients, which is the sum of their squares.
> The lasso estimate is the vector of coefficients with the smallest penalized fit, where the penalty adds up the absolute values.
>
> ✅ The ridge estimate minimizes the residual sum of squares plus a penalty equal to the sum of the squared coefficients.
> The lasso estimate minimizes the residual sum of squares plus a penalty equal to the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients.
> The two definitions differ only in the penalty.

The ❌ pair varies every phrase, so the reader must compare them clause by clause to find that only the penalty differs.
The ✅ pair repeats the shared words and ends by naming the one change.

:::

Rewording is for the places where the meaning differs.
Do not repeat a result for the sake of repetition;
[reuse one written version of each result](teaching.qmd#reuse-one-written-version-of-each-result) covers that case.

No check can decide that two results are parallel,
so this stays a writing rule that review enforces.

# State a theorem in one short sentence

Halmos advises that "the statement of the theorem should consist of one sentence whenever possible",
and that the sentence be a short one
[@halmos1970write, section 10].
Put the introductory comments, preliminary definitions and motivation before the statement,
and the proof after it.
Leave asides out of the statement itself.
Halmos says that phrases such as "without loss of generality we may assume ..."
and "moreover it follows from Theorem 1 that ..."
do not belong in the statement of a theorem
[@halmos1970write, section 10].
A reasoning word in a statement ("so", "because") is a separate fault,
and [Build every unit from smaller atomic units](teaching.qmd#build-every-unit-from-smaller-atomic-units) covers it.

:::{#exm-one-sentence-statement}

# Moving an aside out of a statement

> ❌ Without loss of generality, let $x > 0$.
> Moreover, the sequence converges.
>
> ✅ If $x > 0$, then the sequence converges.

The ❌ statement is two sentences, and the first one is an aside.
The ✅ statement is one implication.
If the case $x < 0$ needs the same argument, say so in the proof.

:::

A statement that lists many hypotheses and many conclusions is too long for one sentence.
Halmos says that "a list of eight hypotheses ... and a list of six conclusions do not a theorem make;
they are a badly expounded theory",
and that the hypotheses "probably describe a general concept that deserves to be isolated, named, and studied"
[@halmos1970write, section 10].
Name the shared concept in its own definition,
and state each conclusion as its own result.

A warn-only check ([gha#1368](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/gha/pull/1368)) flags "without loss of generality", "moreover" and "furthermore" on a line that a pull request adds to a theorem statement.
No check can measure whether a statement is short or whether its hypotheses form a concept,
so the length rule stays a writing rule that review enforces.

# Title a result with the sentence it states

The title of a theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, or conjecture
is a declarative sentence that states the result.
A reader who scans titles,
in a table of contents, a list of results, or a cross-reference,
then learns what each result says without opening it.
A noun phrase such as "Derivative of the logistic function" names a topic <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted title, not a use of the term -->
and leaves the reader to look up what the result says about it.

When a result has a customary name,
such as "Hoeffding's inequality" or "the bias-variance decomposition",
put the name first, then a colon, then the sentence.
The name lets a reader find the result under the name other sources use,
and the sentence says what the result states.

The title may leave out hypotheses that the statement gives,
such as "if the step size is small enough".
The statement itself still stands alone,
as the [State a theorem in one short sentence](#state-a-theorem-in-one-short-sentence) section asks.
This rule covers results only:
a definition's title names the [term](defining-terms.qmd#def-term) it defines,
and an example's title names what the example does.

::: {#exm-result-title-sentence}

# Turning result titles into sentences

These titles come from the [machine learning notes](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/).

> ❌ Derivative of the logistic function <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted title, not a use of the term -->
>
> ✅ The derivative of the logistic function is its value times one minus its value <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted title, not a use of the term -->
>
> ❌ Bias-variance decomposition
>
> ✅ Bias-variance decomposition: the expected squared error of a prediction at an input is its squared bias plus its variance plus the noise variance <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted title, not a use of the term -->

Each ❌ title names what the result is about.
Each ✅ title says what the result states,
and the second keeps the customary name in front of the sentence.

:::

A failing check, [`check-result-titles`](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/gha/pull/2168),
flags a result title on a line that a pull request adds
when the title holds no verb and no math relation.
It tests for verbs with a word list,
so it can flag a sentence whose verb is missing from that list;
such a line takes `<!-- check-result-titles: allow: <reason> -->`,
or the verb goes into the list.

# State the title's sentence again in the statement, in words and in symbols

The statement of a result says what its title says twice more:
once in words, as a sentence close to the title's,
and once in full mathematical notation.
The sentence in words lets a reader check that the statement is the result the title promises,
and the formula is what a reader uses in a calculation or a proof.
Put the sentence first, then the formula in a display.
The sentence adds the hypotheses the title leaves out,
each named in words,
and it names its symbols, so that the formula after it needs no further explanation.

::: {#exm-result-statement-two-forms}

# The logistic derivative in words and in symbols

> ❌ **The derivative of the logistic function is its value times one minus its value** <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted title, not a use of the term -->
>
> For every $\predvar$, $\dexpitf{\predvar} = \expitf{\predvar}\paren{1 - \expitf{\predvar}}$.
>
> ✅ **The derivative of the logistic function is its value times one minus its value** <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted title, not a use of the term -->
>
> At every input $\predvar$, the derivative of the logistic function $\expit$ is the value of $\expit$ at $\predvar$ times one minus that value: <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted statement, not a use of the term -->
>
> $$
> \dexpitf{\predvar} = \expitf{\predvar}\paren{1 - \expitf{\predvar}}.
> $$

The ❌ statement gives only the formula,
so the reader has to translate it back into the title's words to see that the two agree.
The ✅ statement says the title's sentence again with its symbols named,
then gives the same claim as a displayed formula.

:::

The check [`check-result-titles`](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/gha/pull/2168)
also flags a result whose statement, the text of the div before its proof,
has no display formula or no sentence in words.
It cannot tell whether the sentence says what the title says,
since that needs the meaning of both, not their words,
so that part of the rule is applied in review.

Name every hypothesis of a result in words, with its symbol beside it.
The same holds for every condition in a definition.
Write "a nonnegative random variable $X$" and "a positive number $a$",
not "a random variable $X$ with $X \ge 0$" and "for every $a > 0$".
A reader who meets a result first asks when it applies.
A condition written only as an inequality answers that question in symbols,
which the reader has to translate before reading on.
The word ("nonnegative", "finite", "nonzero") also names a property
that the reader can recognize in other results, and look up when it is new.
The formula for a condition may follow its words
where a proof or a later step uses the formula.

::: {#exm-hypotheses-in-words}

# Markov's inequality with its hypotheses in words

> ❌ Let $X$ be a random variable with $X \ge 0$ and $\E{X} < \infty$.
> Then for every $a > 0$:
>
> $$
> \Prf{X \ge a} \le \frac{\E{X}}{a}.
> $$ {#eq-markov-hypotheses-symbols}
>
> ✅ Let $X$ be a nonnegative random variable with a finite expected value $\E{X}$,
> and let $a$ be a positive number.
> Then the probability that $X$ is at least $a$ is at most $\E{X}$ divided by $a$:
>
> $$
> \Prf{X \ge a} \le \frac{\E{X}}{a}.
> $$ {#eq-markov-hypotheses-words}

The ❌ statement gives all three hypotheses as inequalities,
so the reader has to translate each one to learn what the result needs:
a nonnegative random variable, a finite expected value, and a positive threshold.
The ✅ statement names each condition in words,
with its symbol beside it,
and says the conclusion in words before the formula.

:::

The check [`check-result-titles`](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/gha/blob/main/website/reference/check-result-titles.qmd)
flags a result statement that gives a hypothesis as an inline inequality
right after a word such as "with", "where", "if", "let", or "for every".
It cannot tell whether a condition is named in words elsewhere in the sentence,
and it does not read definitions,
so those parts of the rule are applied in review.

# Rules that other chapters cover

@tbl-knuth-elsewhere lists the course's other rules and where this book discusses them.

:::{#tbl-knuth-elsewhere}

Rule | Where it appears
---- | ----------------
Define every variable when you introduce it | [Defining terms](defining-terms.qmd#guidelines-for-defining-terms)
Use one notation for one thing, and one thing for each notation | [Mathematical notation](notation.qmd#matching-names-and-notation)
Motivate a result before you derive it | [Show why you need a result before you derive it](notation.qmd#show-why-you-need-a-result-before-you-derive-it)
Avoid strings of nouns used as adjectives | [Rewrite noun strings and hidden verbs](inclusive-writing.qmd#rewrite-noun-strings-and-hidden-verbs)
Avoid unnecessary jargon | [Minimize unnecessary jargon](word-choice.qmd#minimize-unnecessary-jargon)
Keep "this" and "also" out of consecutive sentences | [Keep "this" and "also" out of consecutive sentences](word-choice.qmd#keep-this-and-also-out-of-consecutive-sentences)
Write sentences that can be read from left to right without ambiguity | [Avoid garden-path sentences](grammar.qmd#avoid-garden-path-sentences)
Use "that" instead of "which" in a [restrictive clause](grammar.qmd#def-restrictive-clause) | [Relative pronouns](grammar.qmd#relative-pronouns)
Do not praise your own work | [Tone](avoid-cliches.qmd#tone)

Rules from the course that other chapters of this book cover

:::
